lesson.title: Double-Blind: Closing Both Doors on Bias
lesson.summary: A double-blind experiment hides treatment assignment from both the subjects and the people administering or evaluating treatment, removing expectation effects from both sides of the study.
lesson.body:
A double-blind experiment extends single-blinding one step further: neither the subjects nor the researchers who interact with them, administer treatments, or measure outcomes know which subjects are in which group. Only someone who is not involved in day-to-day contact with participants, often a study statistician working from coded labels, holds the key connecting subject identities to treatment assignments, and that key typically stays sealed until data collection is complete. The word double counts two blinded parties: the people receiving treatment and the people delivering or scoring it.

The reasoning follows directly from the single-blind discussion. Single-blinding controls the subject's placebo-driven expectations but leaves the researcher's expectations free to leak into the data through subtle cues, tone of voice, or slightly generous scoring. Double-blinding removes that channel too. If the nurse handing out pills does not know whether a given bottle contains the real drug or the placebo, she cannot treat one group more warmly or read their symptoms more favorably, even unintentionally. Both the placebo effect on subjects and the analogous expectation effect on researchers are handled at once, which is why double-blind designs are considered the strongest standard for many clinical trials.

Consider the earlier hypothetical arthritis drug trial, redesigned as double-blind. The pharmacy prepares 200 identical-looking pill bottles labeled only with a code number, not Drug or Placebo. Neither the participants nor the rheumatologist who examines their joints each week knows which code numbers correspond to the real medication. The rheumatologist scores joint swelling and mobility using the same criteria for every participant, with no knowledge of group assignment to bias that scoring, whether favorably or unfavorably. Only after all 200 patients have completed the trial does the study statistician unseal the code and compare outcomes by actual group.

Double-blinding is not always achievable. If one treatment has an obvious, hard-to-disguise side effect, for example a drug that visibly changes skin color, or if a treatment involves surgery versus no surgery, it may be impossible to keep either subjects or evaluators fully unaware. In such cases, researchers use whatever partial blinding is possible, such as having an independent, blinded specialist read scans or lab results without ever meeting the patient, so that at least the measurement step stays protected.

It is worth being precise about what double-blinding does and does not do. It reduces response bias and evaluator bias, both of which are forms of the general problem of bias described earlier in this course. It does not, by itself, guarantee that the treatment groups are comparable at the start of the study; that job belongs to random assignment. A well-run experiment typically uses random assignment to build comparable groups and double-blinding to keep the measurement of those groups honest, two different safeguards aimed at two different problems.
